items.name: Sealed clay contract
items.desc: Mesopotamia. A cylinder seal rolled across a field-sale tablet, binding a named party to a transaction.
items.fail: Forged by anyone holding the seal

items.name: Photographic passport
items.desc: 1922. The League of Nations standard of 1920 fixed the format the world still uses: a book, a photograph, an issuing authority.
items.fail: Only as good as the issuing state

items.name: Nansen passport
items.desc: 1929. Identity for people no state would vouch for, honoured only because other states agreed to accept it.
items.fail: Worth exactly what verifiers granted it

items.name: Social Security number
items.desc: From 1935. An identifier issued for one purpose that became the de facto national identity number for many.
items.fail: Borrowed as an identifier, then used as a secret

cap: Four identity systems separated by nearly four thousand years, and the red line under each is its characteristic failure. Between them they cover the whole ancient list: forgery, dependence on an issuer, dependence on other parties agreeing to honour the thing, and an identifier quietly acquiring uses nobody authorized. Not one is a failure of the artifact. The seal is well made, the passport is well printed, the card is unambiguous. Everything that goes wrong is institutional, and every item on that list is still live.
